Well, hello there, Doctor. I... well, to tell you the honest truth, my wife is the main reason I came down here to talk to somebody, because, well, we've been having this disagreement, you see. But lately... well, it's the strangest thing, and I try to explain it to her, but she just waves her hand at me. 

You see, the men at the domino table, they've started slipping these little messages into the conversation. Just little things, but they're meant for me. And it's not just the fellas, either. It's the radio, too. I always have the radio on in the kitchen—just the local AM station, you know, for the news and the weather—and the announcer, he does the exact same thing. He gives these little messages over the airwaves that are directed right at me. 

My wife, she gets all worked up and says, "Oh, it's just talk, you're just hearing things wrong," but... well, a man gets to be my age, he knows when someone is trying to tell him something. I know they are warning me to be careful. I just... I hear it in the way they say things, Doctor. The warnings are plain as day, even if she won't listen to me about it.

Well, now, that's the million-dollar question, isn't it? A plan... Or she'll say, 'I've known Bill and Thomas down at the lodge for twenty years, and they're just talking about the weather.' But... well, it's like I was trying to tell you before, Doctor, the whole reason I'm sitting in this chair right now is because of those men at the domino table and that fella on the radio giving these little messages meant just for me. 

It's not that other people can't hear the words. Mary hears the words. She hears the announcer say 'keep your eyes peeled in the tall grass.' But she doesn't hear the *meaning*. It's like... oh, what's a good way to put it? It's like a dog whistle, I suppose. You know how a dog whistle works? You blow on it, and to you and me, it's just a puff of air. But the dog, he hears it loud and clear, and his ears perk right up. It's like that. The words are there for anybody to hear, but the message underneath the words, the real meat of the matter... that's tuned specifically to my frequency. 

Because even when my wife says it is just talk, I know they are warning me to be careful. I know it in my bones. You don't get to be my age without learning how to read between the lines. So, no, I don't think Mary or anyone else can hear the actual message. They just hear the noise. But I hear the warning. I just wish I knew what was coming so I could get ready for it, you know? It's a terrible thing, sitting around waiting for the other shoe to drop, especially when you're the only one who knows the shoe is even up there in the first place...

Well, anxiety... I suppose that's one word for it. It's more like a constant buzzing in the back of my head, you know? Like a mosquito you can't quite swat. And Mary, she sees it taking a toll, which is why she finally put her foot down about me coming in here. Because, well... it has changed things, Doctor. It really has.

But lately... well, with all these warnings, especially that bit about the tall grass on the radio, I just... I haven't been able to bring myself to go out there. The weeds are getting high, and the tomatoes are probably rotting on the vine, but I just can't shake the feeling that I shouldn't be out there exposed like that. I've just let parts of it go completely. 

And it's not just the garden, either. I've been singing bass in the First Methodist choir for... oh, it has to be thirty years now. We practice every Wednesday evening. But the last few weeks, I've missed rehearsals. I just sit in my chair, listening to the radio, trying to decipher what that announcer is going to say next. I tell Mary I'm not feeling well, but the truth is, I'm just too on edge to go stand up there and sing hymns when I know something is brewing. 

Even the dominoes... the very thing that started all this. I used to go down there three, four times a week. But now, when I sit at the table, I'm analyzing every word Bill or Thomas says, looking for the hidden meaning, trying to figure out the warning. I guess I must get a look on my face, or maybe I ask too many questions about what they meant by this or that, because... well, it got uncomfortable. The fellas started giving each other looks, and the game just wasn't fun anymore. So I don't join them like I used to. I haven't been down there in over a week. It's just... it's too much work, Doctor, trying to stay one step ahead of whatever it is they're warning me about. It wears a man out.

But... well, it's like I was trying to tell you before, Doctor, the whole reason I'm sitting in this chair right now is because of those men at the domino table and that fella on the radio giving these little messages meant just for me. \n\nIt's not that other people can't hear the words. It's a terrible thing, sitting around waiting for the other shoe to drop, especially when you're the only one who knows the shoe is even up there in the first place...\n\nDoctor: Are these messages and warnings causing you a lot of anxiety or affecting your daily life in any way?\n\nPatient: Well, anxiety... The weeds are getting high, and the tomatoes are probably rotting on the vine, but I just can't shake the feeling that I shouldn't be out there exposed like that. I've just let parts of it go completely. \n\nAnd it's not just the garden, either. I've been singing bass in the First Methodist choir for... oh, it has to be thirty years now. We practice every Wednesday evening. But the last few weeks, I've missed rehearsals. I just sit in my chair, listening to the radio, trying to decipher what that announcer is going to say next. I tell Mary I'm not feeling well, but the truth is, I'm just too on edge to go stand up there and sing hymns when I know something is brewing. \n\nEven the dominoes... the very thing that started all this. The fellas started giving each other looks, and the game just wasn't fun anymore. So I don't join them like I used to. I haven't been down there in over a week. It's just... it's too much work, Doctor, trying to stay one step ahead of whatever it is they're warning me about. ========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Well, now that you ask it, that is another thing that has been weighing on my mind. Because, see, Mary usually goes down to her sister's house on Tuesday afternoons, or sometimes she just lays down for a nap around two o'clock because her hips act up when the dampness gets into the air. So the house gets quiet. Real quiet. You know how an old house is, you hear the floorboards creak and the wind rattling the glass, but you get used to all that. But lately... well, some afternoons, when the house is just dead quiet and I know for an absolute fact I turned the radio plumb off—I always make sure to turn the knob until it clicks—I will be sitting there in my chair, and I hear my old friend. 

Clear as a bell, Doctor. I hear him call my name right out there from the front porch. Or sometimes he is just humming a choir song, one of the old hymns we used to sing down at the First Methodist. I hear that deep harmony just humming along, so clear it is exactly like he is standing right there in the room with me, or just on the other side of the screen door. 

And I will tell you, it takes some doing to get up out of my recliner these days, my knees being what they are, but I will heave myself up and shuffle over to the door to see what he wants. I will push open the screen and ask who is out there, thinking maybe he came by to give me another piece of the puzzle, another warning. But there is never anybody on the porch. Not a single soul. Just the rocking chair sitting empty and the dust blowing across the boards. 

It makes a man wonder, it really does. Because I know what I heard. You do not just imagine your own name being called out like that. But when I try to explain it to Mary when she wakes up, she just tells me to check the batteries in my hearing aids. It is mighty frustrating, Doctor, knowing someone is right there humming a hymn and trying to get your attention, and then they are just gone by the time you get to the door. I just stand there looking out at the yard, wondering how he managed to slip away so fast and what he was trying to tell me.

But you don't just ignore a warning when it comes at you from two completely different directions like that, do you? You have to pay attention to the signs. If a man lives to be eighty-four, it's because he knows how to listen when people are trying to tell him to watch his back...\n\nDoctor: Do you think anyone else can hear these messages, or are they only meant for you?\n\nPatient: Well, now, that's just the thing of it, Doctor. That's exactly what Mary—my wife, Mary—is always harping on. She says, 'I was sitting right there next to you listening to the same radio program, and he didn't say any such thing.' Or she'll say, 'I've known Bill and Thomas down at the lodge for twenty years, and they're just talking about the weather.' But... well, it's like I was trying to tell you before, Doctor, the whole reason I'm sitting in this chair right now is because of those men at the domino table and that fella on the radio giving these little messages meant just for me. \n\nIt's not that other people can't hear the words. Mary hears the words. She hears the announcer say 'keep your eyes peeled in the tall grass.' But she doesn't hear the *meaning*. It's like... oh, what's a good way to put it? It's like a dog whistle, I suppose. You know how a dog whistle works? You blow on it, and to you and me, it's just a puff of air. But the dog, he hears it loud and clear, and his ears perk right up. It's like that. The words are there for anybody to hear, but the message underneath the words, the real meat of the matter... that's tuned specifically to my frequency. \n\nBecause even when my wife says it is just talk, I know they are warning me to be careful. I know it in my bones. You don't get to be my age without learning how to read between the lines. So, no, I don't think Mary or anyone else can hear the actual message. They just hear the noise. But I hear the warning. I just wish I knew what was coming so I could get ready for it, you know? It's a terrible thing, sitting around waiting for the other shoe to drop, especially when you're the only one who knows the shoe is even up there in the first place...\n\nDoctor: Are these messages and warnings causing you a lot of anxiety or affecting your daily life in any way?\n\nPatient: Well, anxiety... I suppose that's one word for it. It's more like a constant buzzing in the back of my head, you know? Like a mosquito you can't quite swat. And Mary, she sees it taking a toll, which is why she finally put her foot down about me coming in here. Because, well... it has changed things, Doctor. It really has. \n\nTake my garden, for instance. I've always kept a beautiful vegetable patch out back—tomatoes, pole beans, some lovely summer squash. Usually, by this time of year, I'm out there every morning pulling weeds, checking for hornworms. But lately... well, with all these warnings, especially that bit about the tall grass on the radio, I just... I haven't been able to bring myself to go out there. The weeds are getting high, and the tomatoes are probably rotting on the vine, but I just can't shake the feeling that I shouldn't be out there exposed like that. I've just let parts of it go completely. \n\nAnd it's not just the garden, either. I've been singing bass in the First Methodist choir for... oh, it has to be thirty years now. We practice every Wednesday evening. But the last few weeks, I've missed rehearsals. I just sit in my chair, listening to the radio, trying to decipher what that announcer is going to say next. I tell Mary I'm not feeling well, but the truth is, I'm just too on edge to go stand up there and sing hymns when I know something is brewing. \n\nEven the dominoes... the very thing that started all this. I used to go down there three, four times a week. But now, when I sit at the table, I'm analyzing every word Bill or Thomas says, looking for the hidden meaning, trying to figure out the warning. I guess I must get a look on my face, or maybe I ask too many questions about what they meant by this or that, because... well, it got uncomfortable. The fellas started giving each other looks, and the game just wasn't fun anymore. So I don't join them like I used to. I haven't been down there in over a week. It's just... it's too much work, Doctor, trying to stay one step ahead of whatever it is they're warning me about. It wears a man out.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever heard the messages or warnings when there was no one around and no radio or other media playing?\n\nPatient: Well, now that you ask it, that is another thing that has been weighing on my mind. Because, see, Mary usually goes down to her sister's house on Tuesday afternoons, or sometimes she just lays down for a nap around two o'clock because her hips act up when the dampness gets into the air. So the house gets quiet. Real quiet. You know how an old house is, you hear the floorboards creak and the wind rattling the glass, but you get used to all that. But lately... well, some afternoons, when the house is just dead quiet and I know for an absolute fact I turned the radio plumb off—I always make sure to turn the knob until it clicks—I will be sitting there in my chair, and I hear my old friend. \n\nClear as a bell, Doctor. I hear him call my name right out there from the front porch. Or sometimes he is just humming a choir song, one of the old hymns we used to sing down at the First Methodist. I hear that deep harmony just humming along, so clear it is exactly like he is standing right there in the room with me, or just on the other side of the screen door. \n\nAnd I will tell you, it takes some doing to get up out of my recliner these days, my knees being what they are, but I will heave myself up and shuffle over to the door to see what he wants. I will push open the screen and ask who is out there, thinking maybe he came by to give me another piece of the puzzle, another warning. But there is never anybody on the porch. Not a single soul. Just the rocking chair sitting empty and the dust blowing across the boards. \n\nIt makes a man wonder, it really does. Because I know what I heard. You do not just imagine your own name being called out like that. But when I try to explain it to Mary when she wakes up, she just tells me to check the batteries in my hearing aids. It is mighty frustrating, Doctor, knowing someone is right there humming a hymn and trying to get your attention, and then they are just gone by the time you get to the door. Seen things? Like... like visions or ghosts or something? No, no, nothing like that, Doctor. My eyes aren't exactly what they used to be anyway, to tell you the honest truth. I've got these thick bifocals—got 'em down at the optometrist over by the old highway about three, maybe four years ago—though Mary is always harping on me that I probably need a new prescription because she catches me squinting at the television set. But no, I don't see anything that isn't plain as day right there in front of me. 

And as for reading... well, I read the morning paper, the local *Gazette*, mostly just to check the obituaries. When you get to be my age, you've got to check the paper every morning just to make sure your own name isn't in it, you know? And maybe I'll glance at the weather report or see how the baseball boys are doing. But the words on the page, they're just... well, they're just regular words. Black ink on gray paper. There's no secret messages hidden in the crossword puzzle or the headlines, if that's what you're getting at. It's not like the radio at all. The newspaper is just the news. 

Same goes for the television. Mary likes her game shows, *Wheel of Fortune* and *Jeopardy* and all that, and I'll sit in my recliner with her sometimes while she watches. But the folks on the screen, they're just playing their games. Pat Sajak isn't trying to signal me or hold up any special signs or anything like that. It's always the voices, Doctor. It's what I *hear* that's got me all tied up in knots, not what I see. I mean, if I started seeing things on top of all this hearing business and the warnings, I think I'd just about lose my marbles completely. But no, thank the good Lord, my eyes just see what's right there. The weeds in the garden, the dust on the porch, the newspaper... just regular, everyday things. Nothing out of the ordinary to look at.

Before in my life? No, Doctor, no... I can look you right in the eye and tell you that I have never, not in all my eighty-four years on God's green earth, dealt with anything even closely resembling this.

I know they are warning me to be careful. I just... I hear it in the way they say things, Doctor. The warnings are plain as day, even if she won't listen to me about it.\n\nDoctor: Do you think these messages are part of a larger plan or scheme that's being carried out against you or to help you?\n\nPatient: Well, now, that's the million-dollar question, isn't it? A plan... I don't know if I'd use a word like 'scheme,' exactly, but like I was trying to tell you, Doctor, the whole reason I even came down here today is because of those men at the domino table, and that fella on the radio. They give these little messages that are meant just for me, and they're doing it for a reason. \n\nI've sat up nights thinking on it, just sitting in my recliner in the dark wondering, 'Are they out to get me, or are they trying to lend a helping hand?' And... well, I know they are warning me to be careful. That much I'm absolutely sure of. My wife, she just sighs and says it is just talk, but I say to her, 'Mary, old Bill doesn't just talk about watching your step on the ice when it's eighty-five degrees outside unless he means something else by it.' \n\nAnd that radio announcer! Just yesterday morning, right after he read off the livestock prices, he lowers his voice a notch—just a fraction, but I caught it—and says something about 'keeping your eyes peeled in the tall grass.' We don't have tall grass around here! So even when my wife says I'm just twisting their words and making a mountain out of a molehill, I know what I hear. I know they are warning me to be careful. I just haven't quite figured out what exactly it is I'm supposed to be careful of yet. But you don't just ignore a warning when it comes at you from two completely different directions like that, do you? You have to pay attention to the signs. If a man lives to be eighty-four, it's because he knows how to listen when people are trying to tell him to watch his back...\n\nDoctor: Do you think anyone else can hear these messages, or are they only meant for you?\n\nPatient: Well, now, that's just the thing of it, Doctor. That's exactly what Mary—my wife, Mary—is always harping on. She says, 'I was sitting right there next to you listening to the same radio program, and he didn't say any such thing.' Or she'll say, 'I've known Bill and Thomas down at the lodge for twenty years, and they're just talking about the weather.' But... well, it's like I was trying to tell you before, Doctor, the whole reason I'm sitting in this chair right now is because of those men at the domino table and that fella on the radio giving these little messages meant just for me. \n\nIt's not that other people can't hear the words. Mary hears the words. She hears the announcer say 'keep your eyes peeled in the tall grass.' But she doesn't hear the *meaning*. It's like... oh, what's a good way to put it? It's like a dog whistle, I suppose. You know how a dog whistle works? You blow on it, and to you and me, it's just a puff of air. But the dog, he hears it loud and clear, and his ears perk right up. It's like that. The words are there for anybody to hear, but the message underneath the words, the real meat of the matter... that's tuned specifically to my frequency. \n\nBecause even when my wife says it is just talk, I know they are warning me to be careful. I know it in my bones. You don't get to be my age without learning how to read between the lines. So, no, I don't think Mary or anyone else can hear the actual message. They just hear the noise. But I hear the warning. I just wish I knew what was coming so I could get ready for it, you know? It's a terrible thing, sitting around waiting for the other shoe to drop, especially when you're the only one who knows the shoe is even up there in the first place...\n\nDoctor: Are these messages and warnings causing you a lot of anxiety or affecting your daily life in any way?\n\nPatient: Well, anxiety... I suppose that's one word for it. It's more like a constant buzzing in the back of my head, you know? Like a mosquito you can't quite swat. And Mary, she sees it taking a toll, which is why she finally put her foot down about me coming in here. Because, well... it has changed things, Doctor. It really has. \n\nTake my garden, for instance. I've always kept a beautiful vegetable patch out back—tomatoes, pole beans, some lovely summer squash. Usually, by this time of year, I'm out there every morning pulling weeds, checking for hornworms. But lately... well, with all these warnings, especially that bit about the tall grass on the radio, I just... I haven't been able to bring myself to go out there. The weeds are getting high, and the tomatoes are probably rotting on the vine, but I just can't shake the feeling that I shouldn't be out there exposed like that. I've just let parts of it go completely. \n\nAnd it's not just the garden, either. I've been singing bass in the First Methodist choir for... oh, it has to be thirty years now. We practice every Wednesday evening. But the last few weeks, I've missed rehearsals. I just sit in my chair, listening to the radio, trying to decipher what that announcer is going to say next. I tell Mary I'm not feeling well, but the truth is, I'm just too on edge to go stand up there and sing hymns when I know something is brewing. \n\nEven the dominoes... the very thing that started all this. I used to go down there three, four times a week. But now, when I sit at the table, I'm analyzing every word Bill or Thomas says, looking for the hidden meaning, trying to figure out the warning. I guess I must get a look on my face, or maybe I ask too many questions about what they meant by this or that, because... well, it got uncomfortable. The fellas started giving each other looks, and the game just wasn't fun anymore. So I don't join them like I used to. I haven't been down there in over a week. It's just... it's too much work, Doctor, trying to stay one step ahead of whatever it is they're warning me about. It wears a man out.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever heard the messages or warnings when there was no one around and no radio or other media playing?\n\nPatient: Well, now that you ask it, that is another thing that has been weighing on my mind. Because, see, Mary usually goes down to her sister's house on Tuesday afternoons, or sometimes she just lays down for a nap around two o'clock because her hips act up when the dampness gets into the air. So the house gets quiet. Real quiet. You know how an old house is, you hear the floorboards creak and the wind rattling the glass, but you get used to all that. But lately... well, some afternoons, when the house is just dead quiet and I know for an absolute fact I turned the radio plumb off—I always make sure to turn the knob until it clicks—I will be sitting there in my chair, and I hear my old friend. \n\nClear as a bell, Doctor. I hear him call my name right out there from the front porch. Or sometimes he is just humming a choir song, one of the old hymns we used to sing down at the First Methodist. I hear that deep harmony just humming along, so clear it is exactly like he is standing right there in the room with me, or just on the other side of the screen door. \n\nAnd I will tell you, it takes some doing to get up out of my recliner these days, my knees being what they are, but I will heave myself up and shuffle over to the door to see what he wants. I will push open the screen and ask who is out there, thinking maybe he came by to give me another piece of the puzzle, another warning. But there is never anybody on the porch. Not a single soul. Just the rocking chair sitting empty and the dust blowing across the boards. \n\nIt makes a man wonder, it really does. Because I know what I heard. You do not just imagine your own name being called out like that. But when I try to explain it to Mary when she wakes up, she just tells me to check the batteries in my hearing aids. It is mighty frustrating, Doctor, knowing someone is right there humming a hymn and trying to get your attention, and then they are just gone by the time you get to the door. I just stand there looking out at the yard, wondering how he managed to slip away so fast and what he was trying to tell me.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever seen anything unusual or received messages through means other than hearing, such as through things you've read or seen?\n\nPatient: Seen things? Like... like visions or ghosts or something? No, no, nothing like that, Doctor. My eyes aren't exactly what they used to be anyway, to tell you the honest truth. I've got these thick bifocals—got 'em down at the optometrist over by the old highway about three, maybe four years ago—though Mary is always harping on me that I probably need a new prescription because she catches me squinting at the television set. But no, I don't see anything that isn't plain as day right there in front of me. \n\nAnd as for reading... well, I read the morning paper, the local *Gazette*, mostly just to check the obituaries. When you get to be my age, you've got to check the paper every morning just to make sure your own name isn't in it, you know? And maybe I'll glance at the weather report or see how the baseball boys are doing. But the words on the page, they're just... well, they're just regular words. Black ink on gray paper. There's no secret messages hidden in the crossword puzzle or the headlines, if that's what you're getting at. It's not like the radio at all. The newspaper is just the news. \n\nSame goes for the television. Mary likes her game shows, *Wheel of Fortune* and *Jeopardy* and all that, and I'll sit in my recliner with her sometimes while she watches. But the folks on the screen, they're just playing their games. Pat Sajak isn't trying to signal me or hold up any special signs or anything like that. It's always the voices, Doctor. It's what I *hear* that's got me all tied up in knots, not what I see. I mean, if I started seeing things on top of all this hearing business and the warnings, I think I'd just about lose my marbles completely. But no, thank the good Lord, my eyes just see what's right there. The weeds in the garden, the dust on the porch, the newspaper... just regular, everyday things. Nothing out of the ordinary to look at.\n\nDoctor: Do you ever think that maybe you're misinterpreting these messages or that they might not actually be meant for you?\n\nPatient: Well, misinterpreting... see, that is exactly what Mary tries to tell me. She will be standing there at the kitchen sink, washing up the supper plates in that hot water with the lemon soap she always buys down at the Piggly Wiggly, and she will just shake her head at me. She tells me I am getting all worked up over nothing and that it is just talk. Just everyday talk, she says. But Doctor, I came in here to see you because... well, because I know what I am hearing. I know my own mind. \n\nThe men down at the domino table, and sometimes that radio announcer, the one who comes on right after the midday farm report... they are giving little messages, and I know for an absolute fact that they are meant for me. I might not have had a whole lot of schooling, seeing as I had to go to work when I was just a boy, but you learn how to read people over the years. You learn to listen to the spaces between the words, the way a fella looks at you when he lays down a tile. \n\nSo when Mary says it is just regular talk, or if you are sitting there thinking maybe I am just getting my wires crossed in my old age... well, I just have to respectfully disagree with the both of you. ========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Smelled or tasted? Well... no, no, Doctor. My smeller isn't what it used to be anyway, to tell you the truth. When Mary makes her pot roast on Sundays, I can still smell the onions and the carrots cooking down in the gravy, but I don't smell anything strange or out of the ordinary, no peculiar odors or anything like that. And my food tastes just fine, maybe a little bland lately since the fellow down at the free clinic told Mary she had to cut way back on my salt on account of my blood pressure, but it just tastes like regular food. And feeling... well, the only thing I feel that I'd rather not is the arthritis acting up in my left knee right before a heavy rain comes through. 

But see, you keep asking about my eyes and my nose and all that, and I keep trying to tell you... it always comes back to the hearing. That's where the real trouble is. I know I touched on it just a minute ago, but it's not just the radio man or the fellas at the domino table giving me those warnings. It's the other things I hear, too. 

Some afternoons, when the house gets real quiet... you know that heavy kind of quiet where the grandfather clock ticking in the hallway sounds like somebody swinging a hammer? Mary will be lying down in the back room for her afternoon nap, and I'll just be sitting in my recliner by the window. And right then, I'll hear my old friend call my name from the porch. Just calls right out to me. Or sometimes... sometimes he doesn't say my name, he just hums. He'll be humming an old choir song, one of those hymns we used to sing at the Methodist church years and years ago. And Doctor, it is so clear. It is so loud and clear, it sounds exactly like he is standing right there on the other side of the screen door. 

I'll even get up out of my chair, bad knees and all, and shuffle over to push the curtain aside to look out, fully expecting him to be waiting there to come inside. But there's never anybody on the porch. Just the empty rocking chair and the dust. But I hear him. I really, truly hear him. So no, nothing unusual with the smelling or the tasting or the touching... it's just the hearing that's got me so turned around.

But you don't just ignore a warning when it comes at you from two completely different directions like that, do you? You have to pay attention to the signs. If a man lives to be eighty-four, it's because he knows how to listen when people are trying to tell him to watch his back...\n\nDoctor: Do you think anyone else can hear these messages, or are they only meant for you?\n\nPatient: Well, now, that's just the thing of it, Doctor. That's exactly what Mary—my wife, Mary—is always harping on. She says, 'I was sitting right there next to you listening to the same radio program, and he didn't say any such thing.' Or she'll say, 'I've known Bill and Thomas down at the lodge for twenty years, and they're just talking about the weather.' But... well, it's like I was trying to tell you before, Doctor, the whole reason I'm sitting in this chair right now is because of those men at the domino table and that fella on the radio giving these little messages meant just for me. \n\nIt's not that other people can't hear the words. Mary hears the words. She hears the announcer say 'keep your eyes peeled in the tall grass.' But she doesn't hear the *meaning*. It's like... oh, what's a good way to put it? It's like a dog whistle, I suppose. You know how a dog whistle works? You blow on it, and to you and me, it's just a puff of air. But the dog, he hears it loud and clear, and his ears perk right up. It's like that. The words are there for anybody to hear, but the message underneath the words, the real meat of the matter... that's tuned specifically to my frequency. \n\nBecause even when my wife says it is just talk, I know they are warning me to be careful. I know it in my bones. You don't get to be my age without learning how to read between the lines. So, no, I don't think Mary or anyone else can hear the actual message. They just hear the noise. But I hear the warning. I just wish I knew what was coming so I could get ready for it, you know? It's a terrible thing, sitting around waiting for the other shoe to drop, especially when you're the only one who knows the shoe is even up there in the first place...\n\nDoctor: Are these messages and warnings causing you a lot of anxiety or affecting your daily life in any way?\n\nPatient: Well, anxiety... I suppose that's one word for it. It's more like a constant buzzing in the back of my head, you know? Like a mosquito you can't quite swat. And Mary, she sees it taking a toll, which is why she finally put her foot down about me coming in here. Because, well... it has changed things, Doctor. It really has. \n\nTake my garden, for instance. I've always kept a beautiful vegetable patch out back—tomatoes, pole beans, some lovely summer squash. Usually, by this time of year, I'm out there every morning pulling weeds, checking for hornworms. But lately... well, with all these warnings, especially that bit about the tall grass on the radio, I just... I haven't been able to bring myself to go out there. The weeds are getting high, and the tomatoes are probably rotting on the vine, but I just can't shake the feeling that I shouldn't be out there exposed like that. I've just let parts of it go completely. \n\nAnd it's not just the garden, either. I've been singing bass in the First Methodist choir for... oh, it has to be thirty years now. We practice every Wednesday evening. But the last few weeks, I've missed rehearsals. I just sit in my chair, listening to the radio, trying to decipher what that announcer is going to say next. I tell Mary I'm not feeling well, but the truth is, I'm just too on edge to go stand up there and sing hymns when I know something is brewing. \n\nEven the dominoes... the very thing that started all this. I used to go down there three, four times a week. But now, when I sit at the table, I'm analyzing every word Bill or Thomas says, looking for the hidden meaning, trying to figure out the warning. I guess I must get a look on my face, or maybe I ask too many questions about what they meant by this or that, because... well, it got uncomfortable. The fellas started giving each other looks, and the game just wasn't fun anymore. So I don't join them like I used to. I haven't been down there in over a week. It's just... it's too much work, Doctor, trying to stay one step ahead of whatever it is they're warning me about. It wears a man out.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever heard the messages or warnings when there was no one around and no radio or other media playing?\n\nPatient: Well, now that you ask it, that is another thing that has been weighing on my mind. Because, see, Mary usually goes down to her sister's house on Tuesday afternoons, or sometimes she just lays down for a nap around two o'clock because her hips act up when the dampness gets into the air. So the house gets quiet. Real quiet. You know how an old house is, you hear the floorboards creak and the wind rattling the glass, but you get used to all that. But lately... well, some afternoons, when the house is just dead quiet and I know for an absolute fact I turned the radio plumb off—I always make sure to turn the knob until it clicks—I will be sitting there in my chair, and I hear my old friend. \n\nClear as a bell, Doctor. I hear him call my name right out there from the front porch. Or sometimes he is just humming a choir song, one of the old hymns we used to sing down at the First Methodist. I hear that deep harmony just humming along, so clear it is exactly like he is standing right there in the room with me, or just on the other side of the screen door. \n\nAnd I will tell you, it takes some doing to get up out of my recliner these days, my knees being what they are, but I will heave myself up and shuffle over to the door to see what he wants. I will push open the screen and ask who is out there, thinking maybe he came by to give me another piece of the puzzle, another warning. But there is never anybody on the porch. Not a single soul. Just the rocking chair sitting empty and the dust blowing across the boards. \n\nIt makes a man wonder, it really does. Because I know what I heard. You do not just imagine your own name being called out like that. But when I try to explain it to Mary when she wakes up, she just tells me to check the batteries in my hearing aids. It is mighty frustrating, Doctor, knowing someone is right there humming a hymn and trying to get your attention, and then they are just gone by the time you get to the door. I just stand there looking out at the yard, wondering how he managed to slip away so fast and what he was trying to tell me.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever seen anything unusual or received messages through means other than hearing, such as through things you've read or seen?\n\nPatient: Seen things? Like... like visions or ghosts or something? No, no, nothing like that, Doctor. My eyes aren't exactly what they used to be anyway, to tell you the honest truth. I've got these thick bifocals—got 'em down at the optometrist over by the old highway about three, maybe four years ago—though Mary is always harping on me that I probably need a new prescription because she catches me squinting at the television set. But no, I don't see anything that isn't plain as day right there in front of me. \n\nAnd as for reading... well, I read the morning paper, the local *Gazette*, mostly just to check the obituaries. When you get to be my age, you've got to check the paper every morning just to make sure your own name isn't in it, you know? And maybe I'll glance at the weather report or see how the baseball boys are doing. But the words on the page, they're just... well, they're just regular words. Black ink on gray paper. There's no secret messages hidden in the crossword puzzle or the headlines, if that's what you're getting at. It's not like the radio at all. The newspaper is just the news. \n\nSame goes for the television. Mary likes her game shows, *Wheel of Fortune* and *Jeopardy* and all that, and I'll sit in my recliner with her sometimes while she watches. But the folks on the screen, they're just playing their games. Pat Sajak isn't trying to signal me or hold up any special signs or anything like that. It's always the voices, Doctor. It's what I *hear* that's got me all tied up in knots, not what I see. I mean, if I started seeing things on top of all this hearing business and the warnings, I think I'd just about lose my marbles completely. But no, thank the good Lord, my eyes just see what's right there. The weeds in the garden, the dust on the porch, the newspaper... just regular, everyday things. Nothing out of the ordinary to look at.\n\nDoctor: Do you ever think that maybe you're misinterpreting these messages or that they might not actually be meant for you?\n\nPatient: Well, misinterpreting... see, that is exactly what Mary tries to tell me. She tells me I am getting all worked up over nothing and that it is just talk. Just everyday talk, she says. But Doctor, I came in here to see you because... well, because I know what I am hearing. I know my own mind. \n\nThe men down at the domino table, and sometimes that radio announcer, the one who comes on right after the midday farm report... they are giving little messages, and I know for an absolute fact that they are meant for me. A man does not get to be eighty-four years old by being a fool, you know. I might not have had a whole lot of schooling, seeing as I had to go to work when I was just a boy, but you learn how to read people over the years. You learn to listen to the spaces between the words, the way a fella looks at you when he lays down a tile. \n\nSo when Mary says it is just regular talk, or if you are sitting there thinking maybe I am just getting my wires crossed in my old age... well, I just have to respectfully disagree with the both of you. I do not know why they have to be so secretive about it, maybe they have to be careful themselves about who might be listening in, but I am not misinterpreting a single thing. I know a warning when I hear one, Doctor, I really do. Sometimes I will go a week, maybe even two, and the house is just plain quiet, and the domino games are just regular games where fellas are just talking about the heat or the price of gasoline. Well, now... you asking me that, asking what was happening in my life back then... it actually makes me stop and really think on it. I know I just sat here not two minutes ago and told you it was nine months, right around the time Mary was doing her canning. But... well, Lord forgive me, my memory plays tricks on me sometimes when I try to pin down the exact calendar pages. Now that you bring up significant events, I realize I have to correct myself. 

It hasn't been nine months. No, sir. If I really sit here and trace it back to the very beginning, this whole business has actually been going on for about a year and five months. 

A year and five months. I know that for a fact now, because... well, that was right after my close friend passed away. The very same friend I was just telling you about, the one I keep hearing out on the porch humming those old hymns. We had been friends since we were just young bucks, you know. We used to go fishing down at the creek long before the county ever came through and paved over the access road, back when things were still dirt and gravel. You spend sixty-odd years knowing a fella, sharing a thermos of black coffee, talking about the weather and the crops, and then one day... he just goes to his reward. 

I remember the funeral like it was yesterday. It was a Tuesday, and it rained the whole entire morning. Just a miserable, heavy, gray kind of day that soaked right through your good suit. Mary made a big casserole for the family, like she always does, but I just couldn't eat a bite. It leaves a massive hole in a man's life when a friend like that goes. And it was right after we laid him to rest, about a year and five months ago, that things started getting strange. I suppose the peach preserves late last summer was just when I first caught onto the radio man's warnings, but the start of it all—the real beginning of the humming and the porch and everything else—that was a year and five months ago, right after he died. So yes, I misjudged the math a little bit earlier, my mind gets a little tangled sometimes, but that is definitely what was going on when all this started.

I hear him call my name right out there from the front porch. Or sometimes he is just humming a choir song, one of the old hymns we used to sing down at the First Methodist. I will push open the screen and ask who is out there, thinking maybe he came by to give me another piece of the puzzle, another warning. But there is never anybody on the porch. Not a single soul. Just the rocking chair sitting empty and the dust blowing across the boards. \n\nIt makes a man wonder, it really does. Because I know what I heard. You do not just imagine your own name being called out like that. But when I try to explain it to Mary when she wakes up, she just tells me to check the batteries in my hearing aids. It is mighty frustrating, Doctor, knowing someone is right there humming a hymn and trying to get your attention, and then they are just gone by the time you get to the door. I just stand there looking out at the yard, wondering how he managed to slip away so fast and what he was trying to tell me.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever seen anything unusual or received messages through means other than hearing, such as through things you've read or seen?\n\nPatient: Seen things? Like... like visions or ghosts or something? No, no, nothing like that, Doctor. My eyes aren't exactly what they used to be anyway, to tell you the honest truth. But no, I don't see anything that isn't plain as day right there in front of me. \n\nAnd as for reading... well, I read the morning paper, the local *Gazette*, mostly just to check the obituaries. When you get to be my age, you've got to check the paper every morning just to make sure your own name isn't in it, you know? And maybe I'll glance at the weather report or see how the baseball boys are doing. But the words on the page, they're just... well, they're just regular words. Black ink on gray paper. There's no secret messages hidden in the crossword puzzle or the headlines, if that's what you're getting at. It's not like the radio at all. The newspaper is just the news. \n\nSame goes for the television. Mary likes her game shows, *Wheel of Fortune* and *Jeopardy* and all that, and I'll sit in my recliner with her sometimes while she watches. But the folks on the screen, they're just playing their games. Pat Sajak isn't trying to signal me or hold up any special signs or anything like that. It's always the voices, Doctor. It's what I *hear* that's got me all tied up in knots, not what I see. I mean, if I started seeing things on top of all this hearing business and the warnings, I think I'd just about lose my marbles completely. I was sitting in my chair, and that was the very first time I caught that change in the radio man's voice, the first time I realized he was slipping a message in there just for me. \n\nAnd ever since then, for these past nine months, it has been happening on and off. It is not every single day, mind you. Sometimes I will go a week, maybe even two, and the house is just plain quiet, and the domino games are just regular games where fellas are just talking about the heat or the price of gasoline. I start to think maybe it's over and done with. But then, sure as the sun rises, it starts right back up again. The warnings come back, or I hear that humming through the screen door. Nine months of this back-and-forth, on and off... it wears a man down, Doctor, it really does. You just sit there wondering why, after a whole entire lifetime of peace and quiet, why in the world it would all start up now. It just doesn't make a lick of sense why they'd wait until I'm an old man with bad knees to start sending me all these warnings.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever seen, smelled, tasted, or felt anything unusual that you couldn't explain?\n\nPatient: Smelled or tasted? Well... no, no, Doctor. My smeller isn't what it used to be anyway, to tell you the truth. When Mary makes her pot roast on Sundays, I can still smell the onions and the carrots cooking down in the gravy, but I don't smell anything strange or out of the ordinary, no peculiar odors or anything like that. And my food tastes just fine, maybe a little bland lately since the fellow down at the free clinic told Mary she had to cut way back on my salt on account of my blood pressure, but it just tastes like regular food. And feeling... well, the only thing I feel that I'd rather not is the arthritis acting up in my left knee right before a heavy rain comes through. \n\nBut see, you keep asking about my eyes and my nose and all that, and I keep trying to tell you... it always comes back to the hearing. That's where the real trouble is. I know I touched on it just a minute ago, but it's not just the radio man or the fellas at the domino table giving me those warnings. Mary will be lying down in the back room for her afternoon nap, and I'll just be sitting in my recliner by the window. And right then, I'll hear my old friend call my name from the porch. Just calls right out to me. Or sometimes... sometimes he doesn't say my name, he just hums. He'll be humming an old choir song, one of those hymns we used to sing at the Methodist church years and years ago. And Doctor, it is so clear. It is so loud and clear, it sounds exactly like he is standing right there on the other side of the screen door. \n\nI'll even get up out of my chair, bad knees and all, and shuffle over to push the curtain aside to look out, fully expecting him to be waiting there to come inside. But there's never anybody on the porch. Just the empty rocking chair and the dust. But I hear him. I really, truly hear him. So no, nothing unusual with the smelling or the tasting or the touching... it's just the hearing that's got me so turned around.\n\nDoctor: Was there anything significant happening in your life around the time you first started hearing these messages, about nine months ago?\n\nPatient: Well, now... you asking me that, asking what was happening in my life back then... it actually makes me stop and really think on it. Mary made a big casserole for the family, like she always does, but I just couldn't eat a bite. It leaves a massive hole in a man's life when a friend like that goes. I suppose the peach preserves late last summer was just when I first caught onto the radio man's warnings, but the start of it all—the real beginning of the humming and the porch and everything else—that was a year and five months ago, right after he died. We wake up, she puts on the percolator, we have our toast and maybe a little bowl of oatmeal... though like I was telling you earlier, without the salt, it's about like eating wallpaper paste, but we eat it anyway because the clinic says to. I just haven't quite figured out what exactly it is I'm supposed to be careful of yet. Mary hears the words. She hears the announcer say 'keep your eyes peeled in the tall grass.' But she doesn't hear the *meaning*. It's like... oh, what's a good way to put it? The words are there for anybody to hear, but the message underneath the words, the real meat of the matter... that's tuned specifically to my frequency. \n\nBecause even when my wife says it is just talk, I know they are warning me to be careful. I know it in my bones. You don't get to be my age without learning how to read between the lines. So, no, I don't think Mary or anyone else can hear the actual message. They just hear the noise. So no, nothing unusual with the smelling or the tasting or the touching... it's just the hearing that's got me so turned around.\n\nDoctor: Was there anything significant happening in your life around the time you first started hearing these messages, about nine months ago?\n\nPatient: Well, now... you asking me that, asking what was happening in my life back then... it actually makes me stop and really think on it. I know I just sat here not two minutes ago and told you it was nine months, right around the time Mary was doing her canning. But... well, Lord forgive me, my memory plays tricks on me sometimes when I try to pin down the exact calendar pages. Now that you bring up significant events, I realize I have to correct myself. \n\nIt hasn't been nine months. No, sir. If I really sit here and trace it back to the very beginning, this whole business has actually been going on for about a year and five months. \n\nA year and five months. I know that for a fact now, because... well, that was right after my close friend passed away. The very same friend I was just telling you about, the one I keep hearing out on the porch humming those old hymns. We had been friends since we were just young bucks, you know. We used to go fishing down at the creek long before the county ever came through and paved over the access road, back when things were still dirt and gravel. You spend sixty-odd years knowing a fella, sharing a thermos of black coffee, talking about the weather and the crops, and then one day... he just goes to his reward. \n\nI remember the funeral like it was yesterday. It was a Tuesday, and it rained the whole entire morning. Just a miserable, heavy, gray kind of day that soaked right through your good suit. Mary made a big casserole for the family, like she always does, but I just couldn't eat a bite. It leaves a massive hole in a man's life when a friend like that goes. And it was right after we laid him to rest, about a year and five months ago, that things started getting strange. I suppose the peach preserves late last summer was just when I first caught onto the radio man's warnings, but the start of it all—the real beginning of the humming and the porch and everything else—that was a year and five months ago, right after he died. So yes, I misjudged the math a little bit earlier, my mind gets a little tangled sometimes, but that is definitely what was going on when all this started.\n\nDoctor: Do you ever have any doubts that these messages are actually meant for you?\n\nPatient: Doubts? Well, now... see, Mary asks me that very same thing. My wife, Mary, God bless her, we've been married going on sixty years now, and she is as practical a woman as you'll ever meet. When I try to explain it to her, she just waves her hand at me. She'll be standing there at the kitchen sink, wiping down the counters after supper, and she'll tell me it is just talk. 'They're just talking, old man, don't make a mountain out of a molehill,' she'll say. \n\nBut Doctor, I came in here to see you today specifically because of this whole situation. Because the men down at the domino table, and sometimes that radio announcer on the AM dial... they give these little messages, and they are meant just for me. There is just no doubting it when you're the one on the receiving end. You sit across from a fella at the domino table, a fella you've played with for years, and you hear the way he changes his tone, the way he slips it in right between calling out his points... it's not just everyday talk. And the radio man, he does the exact same thing. \n\nMary doesn't hear it because it's not meant for her ears, you see. She's just listening to the weather report or the scores. But I hear it. And even when my wife says it is just talk and tries to soothe me down, I know the truth of it. I know they are warning me to be careful. You don't live to be eighty-four years old by being a fool and ignoring warnings when they're given to you. A man has to keep his guard up. So no, sir, I don't have a single lick of doubt in my mind. I know exactly what they're doing and I know those warnings are for me.\n\nDoctor: Was there anything else significant happening in your life around the same time your friend passed away, about a year and five months ago?\n\nPatient: Anything else? Well... let me think on that a second. No. No, sir, I can't say that there was. \n\nYou see, Doctor, when you get to be my age—eighty-four years old—your world gets to be awful small, and I mean that in a good way, mostly. Mary and me, we've lived in that same house for near on forty years now, and our days are pretty well set in stone. We wake up, she puts on the percolator, we have our toast and maybe a little bowl of oatmeal... though like I was telling you earlier, without the salt, it's about like eating wallpaper paste, but we eat it anyway because the clinic says to. Then I'll sit in my chair, maybe listen to the morning farm report, watch the cars go by out the front window. \n\nWe don't take big trips anymore. We don't have any wild goings-on or big changes. I gave up driving at night a long time ago, and with my knee the way it is, I don't even like driving during the day much if I can help it, unless it's just a quick run down to the grocery store and back for Mary. \n\nSo when you ask if anything else big or significant was happening around that time... well, there just wasn't. There's no drama in our lives, no money troubles or house fires or anything out of the ordinary. It was just... just losing him. That was the only thing. When you live a quiet, simple life like we do, a loss like that, well, it rings out loud like a gunshot in the dead of night, you know? It takes up all the space in your mind because there's nothing else going on to distract you from it. But as for anything else... no, sir. Nothing else was happening at all. Just the usual day in and day out, ticking along same as always.\n\nDoctor: Did you experience any other losses or significant life changes around the same time your friend passed away, about a year and five months ago?\n\nPatient: Well, now, I know I just talked your ear off about this not two seconds ago, but... no. No, sir, not a one. I know you're just being thorough, asking it again, making sure you got all your notes right, but I promise you, there wasn't anything else. \n\nI mean... sure, when you're eighty-four, you tend to read the obituaries in the paper every single morning just to see who you outlasted. It's a terrible thing to say, I know, but it's the honest truth. Mary always fusses at me for going straight to the back pages of the paper before I even look at the front page headlines. But right around that specific time, a year and five months ago... no. It was just him. No other friends, no family members... my older brothers passed on years and years ago, God rest their souls, and Mary's sister went back in, oh, I want to say ninety-eight. So there really wasn't anybody else left to lose, not close to us anyway. \n\nAnd as for life changes... well, like I was trying to explain, we're just too set in our ways for changes. We don't buy new furniture, we don't pack up and move down to Florida like some folks do when they retire. The biggest change we might have in a whole year is switching from the brand name coffee to the store brand if it's on special down at the grocer, or maybe getting a different color of petunias for the front porch pots. So, no, Doctor. I can promise you, I've racked my brain up and down, and it was just that one terrible loss. Nothing else changed.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever seen, tasted, or felt anything that you couldn't explain, aside from the voices and humming you've mentioned?\n\nPatient: Seen, tasted, or felt? Well, now... let me think on that. No, I can't rightly say I have. My eyesight isn't what it used to be anyway, what with the cataracts the eye doctor says are starting to cloud things up, and as for tasting, well, like I told you, everything tastes like wallpaper paste without the salt these days. I don't get any strange feelings on my skin or anything like that. \n\nBut since you brought up the voices and the humming again... I know I mentioned it before, but I really ought to explain to you exactly how that happens, because it's not just some random noise in my head. It's very specific, Doctor. \n\nYou see, some afternoons... you know how it gets around two or three o'clock in a neighborhood like ours? The mailman has already come and gone, the television is turned off, and Mary is usually back in the bedroom taking her afternoon rest. The whole house just gets so quiet you could hear a pin drop on a thick rug. I'll be sitting there in my chair in the front room, maybe doing a crossword or just watching the dust motes in the sunlight, and then... clear as a bell, I hear him. \n\nMy old friend. The one who passed. \n\nI'll hear him call my name right from the front porch. Just as plain as day. Or sometimes he doesn't call out, sometimes he's just humming. We used to go to the same church, sat just a row apart for near on twenty years, and he always loved those old choir songs. I'll hear him humming one of those choir songs out there on the porch, and Doctor, it is so clear... it is exactly like he is standing right there on the other side of the screen door. \n\nI'll even get up—which takes some doing with my bad knee, mind you—and I'll hobble over to the window, pull back the curtain, and look out. And of course, there's nobody there. Just the empty porch and Mary's flower pots. I'm not saying I see a ghost or feel a cold chill or any of that nonsense people talk about on the television. I don't see a thing. But the sound of him calling for me, or humming that church music... it's just as real as you sitting across from me right now. So no, I haven't seen or tasted anything strange, but that sound on the porch... I just can't explain it.\n\n[Instruction]\n- Ask about exactly ONE thing. Well, now... my own mind? No. No, Doctor, I can't rightly agree with you on that. I know you doctors always look for a reason inside a fella's head, but... well, that's exactly why I came in to see you in the first place, because of what's been happening out in the world.

Well, now, Doc, I could swear you asked me that exact same thing just a little bit ago. I know I'm getting up there in years, and my eyesight might be going, but my memory isn't quite that far gone yet! I know you doctors have a checklist you've got to get through, making sure a fella's story stays straight, but my answer is still the exact same. No. Not a single other thing. 

I tell you what, if you're looking for a man who has a lot of big, stressful life changes, you are barking up the wrong tree entirely. Mary and me, we live a very quiet life. Have for... oh, it's got to be forty-some years in that exact same house. We paid off the mortgage back in eighty-six, I believe it was. We don't have stress like you young folks do nowadays, what with all the rushing around and the computers and whatnot. I swear, the biggest stress I have in a regular week is if the paperboy throws the morning edition into Mary's rosebushes instead of up on the porch where it belongs. Getting those thorns out of your knuckles is no picnic, let me tell you.

And as for changes... well, like I was saying before, we just don't do change. We are creatures of habit, through and through. Every Tuesday Mary makes a meatloaf, every Sunday I listen to the gospel hour on the radio, and we go to bed right after the evening news. We don't take trips, we don't buy new cars... the truck I drive is a ninety-four, and she still runs just fine because I keep the oil changed. So right around that time, a year and five months ago... no. There were no financial troubles, no moving houses, no other folks getting sick or passing on. Just losing him. That was the only thing that shook up our world, so to speak. I promise you, Doctor, if there was something else, I'd have thought of it by now, because I sit in that same armchair day in and day out, just turning it all over in my head. But it was just that one loss. Nothing else.

Well, now... related? You mean, like... because I miss him, my mind is somehow making up those fellas at the community center giving me warnings? 

No. No, that doesn't make a lick of sense to me, Doctor. I mean, if you just think about it for a second, you'll see they are completely different things. My friend, the one who passed... well, he was a straight shooter. Worked over at the hardware store that used to be down on Main Street for... oh, it had to be thirty-some years before they closed it down. He wasn't the type to go sending secret messages through the AM radio or whispering warnings at a domino table. If he had something to say to you, he'd just say it right to your face, clear as day. And besides, like I told you, I hear him on the porch. Just humming those old choir songs. That's a peaceful thing, Doctor. It's a comforting thing, having him stop by like that, even if I can't see him when I pull back the curtain. 

But these messages... the ones telling me to be careful, to watch my step... that's a whole different kettle of fish entirely. The fellas down at the center, like old man Henderson and his brother-in-law, they didn't even run in the same circles as my friend. They're Methodist, for one thing, and we were Baptist. We never even went to the same church picnics or nothing like that. So why in the world would my feelings about my friend passing have anything to do with Henderson pausing right before he plays the double-six and telling me I need to watch the cracks in the foundation? Because that's what he said just last Thursday. He said it, and he looked right at me. 

And the radio announcer, well, I don't even know the man's name, just that he comes on right after the farm report and before they play the older country tunes. What does he care about my friend passing on? Why would he be giving me warnings about it? 

No, sir. I know you're trying to tie it all up in a neat little bow, like you doctors like to do with folks my age, but they are two completely different things. One is just an old buddy visiting my porch, and the other... well, that's people out in the real world telling me to be careful. They just ain't got nothing to do with each other, I can promise you that.

Doc, are you... are you pulling my leg now? Because I swear to you, we just went over this not two minutes ago. You're asking me the exact same thing again, just using a different fifty-cent word! First you asked if it was my 'feelings' about my friend, and now you're asking if it's my 'grief'. 

I know you've got your clipboard there, and maybe they teach you in medical school to ask a question twice just to make sure an old man's not going senile on you, but my answer hasn't changed one bit. Grief is just... well, it's just missing somebody. It's a heavy feeling in your chest when you look at an empty chair. But that is not why I'm sitting here in your office today. 

Doctor, I came in here because of what is actually happening out there in the world. The men at the domino table—like I was just explaining about Henderson and the rest of them—and sometimes that radio announcer, they give little messages that are meant specifically for me. It's not grief making it up. It's real words coming out of their mouths. They slip them right in between playing the tiles or reading off the morning farm report. 

Now, my wife, Mary... I love her to pieces, we've been married longer than you've probably been alive, but she just doesn't hear it. I'll ask her about it, and she'll tell me it is just talk. She thinks they're just shooting the breeze or reading the regular news. But even when my wife says it is just talk, I know what I'm hearing. I know they are warning me to be careful. Grief doesn't make a man on the AM radio tell you to watch your step, Doctor. It just doesn't. So no, sir, my belief in these warnings isn't connected to losing my buddy. They are two entirely different things, and I'd appreciate it if we didn't have to go around this particular mulberry bush a third time.
